extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics majors, mathematics instructors, and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Strategies and criteria for how undergraduate mathematics students should read and understand mathematical proofs, and how instructors/researchers can evaluate/encourage those reading practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trying to prove a theorem before reading its proof
rubrics_metrics.description: For each theorem, attempt to think about or try to prove the theorem yourself before reading the presented proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: helps the reader identify high-level goals and structure of the proof, and to see why particular techniques are used. Example transcript: students who tried to prove the claim about 4x^3 - x^4 + 2 sin x = 30 began by analyzing dominating terms and bounds, which matched the high-level ideas of the formal proof. Effect: facilitated 'structuring' the proof and understanding proof techniques (e.g., contraposition) and novel techniques that may be useful elsewhere. Survey evidence: 88% of surveyed mathematicians preferred that students use this strategy, but only 31% of mathematics majors reported using it. Anti-pattern: reading a proof as an aimless sequence of inferences without first forming expectations about goal and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing the assumptions and conclusions with the proof technique being used
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading a proof, explicitly consider what is being assumed, what is being concluded, and which proof technique (e.g., direct, contrapositive, contradiction) is being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: attend to the proof framework to avoid mistaking a proof of a converse or other incorrect structure for a valid proof. Example: students identified when a proof was using contrapositive reasoning and distinguished it from a converse. Survey evidence: 64% of mathematicians preferred students use this approach, but only 33% of mathematics majors reported doing so. Anti-pattern: focusing only on line-by-line derivations and missing the overall proof framework; accepting arguments that prove the converse because one ignored assumptions/conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking a longer proof into parts or sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition long proofs into smaller parts or sub-proofs and treat each part as a unit of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: makes higher-level structure visible, aids summarization and comprehension of the proof's main components. Example transcript: students drew horizontal partitions to mark sub-parts of a proof and labeled where one subproof ended and another began. Survey evidence: 88% of mathematicians preferred this strategy for students, but only 38% of mathematics majors reported using it. Anti-pattern: attempting to understand a long proof solely by verifying how each line follows from previous lines without recognizing modular structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing the proof approach to one's own approach
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the proof, compare the method used to how you would have approached or attempted the proof yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: helps learners acquire new techniques and problem-solving approaches by noticing differences and clever moves they would not have thought of. Example transcript: students noted that a proof's decomposition was clever and different from how they would have approached the problem, and reported that such comparison 'gives you new techniques.' Survey evidence: 87% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 26% of mathematics majors reported doing so. Anti-pattern: passively reading methods without reflecting on alternatives or transferable techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an example to understand a confusing inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When puzzled by a general assertion in a proof, instantiate it with a concrete numerical or specific example to see what the assertion is claiming and why it holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: helps interpret general statements and clarify the meaning of assertions (e.g., divisibility statements). Example transcript: to understand 'if d is a divisor of n then n/d is also a divisor of n', a student used 7 and 21 to see the partner factor 3. Survey evidence: 77% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 43% of mathematics majors reported using it. Anti-pattern: insisting one must only follow formal derivations and refusing to check plausibility by example; note that examples do not prove the statement but can aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension model (Mejia-Ramos et al., 2012): local and holistic understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a proof can be assessed at two levels — local and holistic. Local understanding consists of: (a) knowing the meaning of terms and statements within the proof, (b) being able to justify how new assertions follow from previous ones, (c) understanding how assumptions and conclusions relate to the proof method. Holistic understanding consists of: (a) providing a summary emphasizing high-level goals, (b) applying the proof methods in other situations to prove new theorems, (c) breaking the proof into sub-proofs, (d) applying general proof methods to specific examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: offers evaluative dimensions for what it means to 'understand' a proof. The paper uses this model to generate comprehension questions and to select strategies that promote both local and holistic understanding. Guidance: teaching and assessment should attend to both local (line-level correctness and meaning) and holistic (structure, transfer, summary) components. Note: conventional linear presentations of proofs often obscure holistic aspects; readers must actively construct connections to achieve holistic understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical functions of proofs: beyond mere conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical proofs should not merely convince students that a theorem is true but should provide explanations (why the result holds) and expose techniques useful for solving other problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: proofs that only convince have limited pedagogical value because students may accept truth from authority; pedagogical proofs should aim to give insight and transferable methods. Evidence and context: cited literature (Hanna, Hersh, Yopp, Weber) argues proofs presented to students should serve these broader purposes. Implication: when evaluating or presenting proofs for learning, prioritize explanatory clarity and transferability, not only formal correctness.
